snippet.title: The Day Shakespeare’s Globe Theatre Burned Down | Fire, Ale & “Henry VIII” (1613)
snippet.description: On June 29, 1613, London’s iconic Globe Theatre was packed for a performance of Shakespeare’s Henry VIII. A cannon fired to announce the king’s entrance dramatic, yes, but also disastrous. The blast set the thatched roof on fire, and within an hour, the entire theatre was reduced to ashes. No one died, but one unlucky guy’s pants caught fire he famously put it out with a mug of ale. The Globe, home to Shakespeare’s most legendary plays, burned down in a blaze of history, but was rebuilt the next year.

This historical reconstruction covers the rise of Carthage, the legacy of Hannibal, Roman fear after the Punic Wars, the siege of Carthage, Scipio Aemilianus, and the final destruction of the city. Built in a cinematic 2D animation style, this video aims to present the story in a dramatic but historically grounded way.

Topics covered in this video:

* Carthage and the Punic Wars

* Why Rome wanted Carthage destroyed

snippet.title: Why the Tiger I Carried More Than Armor-Piercing Shells
snippet.description:
The Tiger I carried both armor-piercing and high-explosive 88 mm ammunition during World War II. While armor-piercing rounds were intended for armored targets, high-explosive shells were used against infantry, field fortifications, and other soft targets. This combination gave the Tiger I greater flexibility in different combat situations.

snippet.title: How Rome Provoked a Monster - The Siege of Saguntum 219 BC
snippet.description:
Before the elephants, before the Alps, and before Cannae... Rome made a fatal mistake. Discover the true story of the Siege of Saguntum (219 BC), the spark that ignited the Second Punic War and unleashed Hannibal Barca upon the Roman Republic.

🔥 SUBSCRIBE for more Legendary History: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCRkzCJ23QLHyKN3FCym7c1A

In this episode: History tells us Hannibal hated Rome, but did Rome actually start the fight? We dive into the chaotic geopolitics of the 3rd Century BC to uncover how a broken treaty and a "bad ally" moment turned a local Spanish conflict into a Mediterranean World War.

From Hamilcar’s blood oath to the starving defenders of Saguntum being left on "read" by the Roman Senate, this is the story of how arrogance blinded a superpower. Witness the moment diplomacy failed and Fabius Maximus delivered the most famous ultimatum in ancient history: "I give you War."

⚔️ Key Battles & Events Covered:

The Rise of the Barcids in Spain (New Carthage).

The Ebro Treaty violation.

The brutal 8-month Siege of Saguntum.

The fall of the city and the "Bonfire of Wealth."

Rome's declaration of war in the Carthaginian Senate.

snippet.title: The Pope Who Put a Corpse on Trial: The Bizarre Cadaver Synod of 897
snippet.description: In one of the most disturbing events in papal history, Pope Stephen VI exhumed his dead rival, Pope Formosus, and put his corpse on trial. Dressed in papal robes and propped on a throne, Formosus was accused, found guilty, had his fingers cut off, and was thrown into the Tiber River—all over political grudges. Known as the Cadaver Synod, this grotesque courtroom drama sparked riots and ended with Stephen VI being strangled to death. Yes, this actually happened—and it’s one of the strangest trials in history.

snippet.title: Rome vs Macedonia: The Fall of Greek Kingdoms
snippet.description:
When Alexander the Great’s empire collapsed, Greece was left divided — proud, wounded, and waiting for a savior.
From the ashes of his legacy rose the kingdom of Macedonia, still clinging to the glory of the past. But in the west, a new power was rising — silent, disciplined, and unstoppable.

This is the story of Rome vs Macedonia — the battle between Alexander’s heirs and the future masters of the world.
From the ambitions of King Philip V, to the desperate courage of Perseus, and the cunning strategy of Rome’s legions, this was not just a war for land… it was a war for history itself.

⚔️ The phalanx met the legion.
⚔️ Greece met Rome.
⚔️ And the ancient world changed forever.

Through the blood-soaked hills of Cynoscephalae and the devastating defeat at Pydna, witness how Rome crushed the last defenders of Alexander’s dream — and how Greece, even in ruin, conquered Rome in spirit.

“The swords of Rome ruled the world… but the words of Greece would rule it forever.”

🎥 A cinematic retelling of the fall of the Greek kingdoms and the rise of the Roman Empire — told through emotion, tragedy, and the echoes of glory that shaped civilization.

snippet.title: 6. Easter Island - Where Giants Walked
snippet.description:
SUPPORT THE SHOW AND WATCH AD-FREE: http://patreon.com/fallofcivilizations_podcast

On one of the world’s most isolated islands, hundreds of vast stone statues lie mouldering in the grass. 

In this episode, we take a look at one of archaeology’s most enduring puzzles: the mystery of Easter Island. Find out how this unique community grew up in complete isolation, severed from the rest of the world by a vast expanse of ocean. Discover the incredible story of how it survived for so many centuries, and examine the evidence about what happened to finally bring this society, and its statues, crashing down.

This episode, we're joined by children from the Toki School of Music and Arts on Rapa Nui, who were kind enough to record some traditional ancestral chants especially for the podcast. 

Since 2012, Toki has offered children & adolescents free classes in classical and traditional music, with the aim of keeping the traditions of the island alive.

It's an incredible project, and if you want to help keep it running, you can donate here: https://tokirapanui.org/en/

snippet.title: New Unit Cohesion Mechanic for Total War: Medieval 3 (Idea)
snippet.description:
A new proposed "Unit Cohesion" mechanic for Total War: Medieval 3. With the War Core engine and the early development stage of the game, I figured it was time to open a discussion on how to improve historical combat for Total War. Link to presentation: https://miro.com/app/board/uXjVGTtlPgE=/?share_link_id=304447018859

The Problem:
Historical battles have stagnated due to low unit variety and limited paths to victory (always hammer and anvil). The binary nature of morale also means that nothing mechanically happens to a unit before it flees, leading to boring and grinding gameplay.

The Solution:
Introduce a new "unit cohesion" mechanic that fundamentally changes a unit's behavior prior to being routed to allow for more unit differentiation and tactical options.

The Definition:
"Unit Cohesion" is the degree to which individuals act as a unit. This is very important for historical accuracy where the armies were indeed made of individuals whose ability to win was dictated by the leader's ability to command and control them properly. In fact, most battles were won or lost based on this cohesion rather than casualties.

How it works:
Each unit will now have a Unit Leader that serves as the anchor of the unit and to which the other soldiers of that unit are magnetized to. The level of cohesion of a unit dictates how efficiently these soldiers follow the orders of the leader. So if you give an order, the leader goes first, followed by the rest of the men in a response time proportional to their cohesion. In terms of movement, cohesion degrades the farther and faster you go. When a unit stops moving, it can regain cohesion. For combat, a unit's cohesion dictates how effectively it can fight an opponent. More cohesion (and other factors) mean you can push other unit back. More cohesion mean you can withstand cavalry charges.  

Micro Cohesion:
We need an ability to customize units to improve their cohesion stats. This should include a way to select a unit leader and also a support staff (officers, musicians, bannermen) who can improve a unit's cohesion. There should be tools to visualize and test cohesion outside of actual battles such as a "Training Ground" mode.

Macro Cohesion:
A battle line now becomes much more fluid and dynamic as each unit's engagement ebbs and flows based on their cohesion. Generals and other abilities can help influence the state of cohesion of their forces. There should also be a cohesion system for unit's within larger formations. This could work like Carthay's Harmony system.

snippet.title: Why Cuba Became One of the World’s Most Struggling Nations
snippet.description:
Discover the history of Cuba, from Indigenous Caribbean communities and Columbus’s arrival in 1492 to Spanish conquest, sugar plantations, slavery, independence struggles, José Martí, American influence, Batista, Fidel Castro, the Cuban Revolution, the Cold War, the Special Period, and modern Cuba.

Cuba’s story is not just the story of an island. It is the story of empire, sugar, slavery, resistance, revolution, exile, survival, music, identity, and a people who never stopped fighting to define themselves.

In this documentary, David takes you through the major turning points in Cuban history and explains how one small island became one of the most unforgettable places in the modern world.
